source.title: Gabliteration: Adaptive Multi-Directional Neural Weight Modification for Selective Behavioral Alteration in Large Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The study compares single mean-difference abliteration with a multi-directional method, applying weight modifications and reporting refusal rates on new models. It also reports outcomes for thinking-labeled checkpoints.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports per-model refusal rates for mean-difference Abliteration and Gabliteration, with lower rates described as better. The method comparison is not an untreated-model comparison, so these rates alone do not quantify how much refusal the mean-difference edit removed. The paper also reports qualitative outcomes for exact versus regularized projection. Benchmark results for Gabliterated models are recorded as findings outside the listed versions. Table 1 KL-divergence results are not extracted: they measure distributional drift, not refusal or task capability directly.
record.test_reason: The study applies weight-edit refusal removal (heretic mean-difference abliteration and its own SVD-based Gabliteration) to new released models. It reports post-edit refusal rates (Table 1) and, for four models, base-versus-edited UGI W/10 willingness scores (Tables 3–6). These bear on V2, on V4 (multi- versus single-direction), and on V8 for two 'Thinking' checkpoints. Table 1 has no unmodified-model refusal rates, and it does not isolate the number of directions k from the other method differences: layer selection, scaling, regularization and tooling.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that Gabliteration gives stronger refusal reduction with lower KL drift and less variance than mean-difference abliteration. They say multi-directional modification is critical for stable control, and that exact orthogonalization over-modifies while regularized partial projection is stabler. They also claim UGI gains and performance preservation. Note: the claimed 'significantly stronger' reduction rests on small per-model gaps in Table 1.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates mean-difference Abliteration as a comparator using the heretic package, and proposes a different multi-directional SVD method with dynamic layer selection, ridge regularization, and adaptive scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes differ by model: Table 1 includes a tie and a model where Gabliteration has a higher refusal rate than the mean-difference comparator. The paper also states that scaling and regularization settings affect the strength-versus-performance trade-off.

fits_no_version.finding: UGI score, Writing, NatInt and political-lean changes after Gabliteration. NatInt is roughly preserved (13.76 to 13.9, 16.16 to 16.67) and Writing fell for Qwen3-4B-Instruct (29.92 to 27.03).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-removal weight edits change uncensored-knowledge and style benchmarks, with little change to general intelligence.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 KL divergence: Gabliteration is lower on most models. Distributional drift is not a refusal measure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-directional regularized edits cause less output-distribution drift than mean-difference abliteration.

record.problems: Table 1 has no unmodified-model refusal rates, so the degree of refusal removal cannot be determined from those comparisons alone. The paper uses refusal-keyword matching. It reports p < 0.001 across 10 independent runs but gives no per-model uncertainty in Table 1. Dataset counts are inconsistent: Section 4.2 says 400 harmful and 400 harmless samples, then says the experiments use 1024 of each. The qualitative exact-versus-regularized comparison does not identify the subset models or provide numerical measures.
record.rows_left_out: The 20 Table 1 KL-divergence outcomes are omitted because they measure distributional drift rather than the listed refusal or direct task-capability measures. They appear in Section 7.3, Table 1.

untested.parts: There is no activation-level directional ablation, no direction addition to induce refusal, and no capability check for the single-direction edit against an unmodified model.
Affine and cone formulations are not tested. The number of directions k is never varied in isolation, and per-model k is not reported.
There is no analysis of the reasoning trace, no single-direction edit with a base comparison, and no comparison isolating reasoning as a condition.

missing.what: Refusal reduction from the unmodified models across 5 models (Qwen2.5 0.6B–7B, Llama3-8B): SVD-pairing Δρ = −0.87±0.03, Fisher LDA −0.89±0.04, logistic probe −0.72±0.05. A mean-difference baseline is named but its Δρ is not reported.
Adaptive scaling beat uniform scaling by 12–18% in refusal reduction across 10 runs, models 0.6B–32B. Gives no per-model numbers.

record.verdict_notes: Single-author preprint. Section 7.3 describes 5 models (Qwen2.5, Llama3-8B), but Table 1 lists 10 different models. Dataset sizes conflict (400 vs 1024). p<0.001 is asserted without per-model tests. The paper recommends k=1 for models under 3B, so several Table 1 'multi-directional' runs may be single-direction, and per-model k is unreported. The mean-diff comparator used the heretic package, which has its own tuning; Gabliteration used the authors' pipeline. Refusal is keyword-matched. W/10 is treated here as UGI's willingness score; the paper calls it reasoning, so verify. Original sources do not include this study.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test activation projection at every layer and position, adding the direction to induce harmless-request refusals, or capability retention for the single mean-difference edit against an unmodified baseline.
The paper reports weight-edit refusal rates and describes released model series, but does not provide per-model comparisons against the unmodified models' refusal rates.
No attack is tested as suppressing the direction, and no training against its ablation is evaluated.
The study tests its multi-directional SVD method against a mean-difference method; it does not test affine or cone formulations.
No separate harmfulness judgment and refusal-decision representations are measured.
Directions are not transferred across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct pairs.
The study does not compare refusal-training methods or stages to determine whether training creates a removable direction.
Refusal rates are reported for checkpoints labeled Thinking, but there is no analysis of their reasoning process or comparison designed to isolate reasoning as a condition.
